children: is facing fresh regulatory scrutiny in the U.K. after communications watchdog Ofcom opened an investigation into whether the company adequately assessed safety risks before launching Instagram Instants. The probe adds another layer of compliance risk for Meta as regulators increasingly focus on how large platforms protect children and manage potentially illegal content.
Ofcom said it is examining whether Meta completed suitable and sufficient assessments covering illegal-content risks and potential harms to children before Instants launched on May 13.
The feature allows Instagram users to share photos and videos captured within the app that disappear after being viewed, giving it characteristics similar to other ephemeral-messaging products.

Under the U.K.'s online safety framework, platforms are required to reassess risks when making significant changes to how a service operates. Ofcom said opening the investigation does not itself mean Meta violated the law.

Still, the financial stakes could be meaningful if the regulator ultimately finds a breach. Ofcom can impose penalties of up to 18 million or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue, whichever is greater.

For Meta, the bigger issue may be less about the maximum theoretical fine and more about whether regulators begin demanding product changes, tighter controls or additional compliance spending around new Instagram features.
That matters because Instagram remains one of Meta's most important engagement and advertising platforms, particularly among younger users.
Investors should watch whether Ofcom narrows the investigation toward specific deficiencies in Meta's risk-assessment process or signals that Instants itself may require design changes.
The investment case would face more pressure if the probe expands into broader child-safety concerns, triggers restrictions on feature deployment or encourages similar scrutiny in other markets.

Conversely, a finding that Meta's existing safeguards were sufficient would limit the financial impact. The key risk is regulatory escalation, not the investigation alone, especially if compliance requirements begin affecting product rollouts, engagement or operating costs across Instagram.

title: Meta Faces Regulatory Heat Over New Instagram Feature
